name: Yuksom
tagline: Sikkim's first capital and the trailhead for Goecha La
meta_description: Yuksom guide: Norbugang coronation throne, Dubdi monastery, Kathok lake, the Goecha La and Dzongri treks, homestays, permits, costs and how to get there.
summary: Yuksom is a village at about 1,780 m in West Sikkim where the first Chogyal was crowned in 1642. It holds the Norbugang coronation site, Kathok lake and Dubdi, Sikkim's oldest monastery. It is also the trailhead for Dzongri and Goecha La. No permit is needed for Indians in the village; treks need park permits.
intro: Yuksom sits on a broad, gentle shelf in the forest, the road ending here at the foot of the Kangchenjunga range. Houses, small lodges and fields spread across the slope, with prayer flags at every turn. It is quiet, green and cooler than Pelling, and for many trekkers it is the last village before a week in the mountains.

In 1642 three lamas gathered here and consecrated Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal of Sikkim, beginning a dynasty that ruled until 1975. The name Yuksom is usually explained as the meeting place of the three lamas. The coronation site at Norbugang, with a stone throne, a chorten and a large cypress tree, lies a short walk above the bazaar, next to the small Kathok lake.

On the hill above the village, Dubdi monastery, founded in 1701, is counted as the oldest monastery in Sikkim. Beyond it, the trail climbs into Khangchendzonga National Park, a World Heritage Site, towards Dzongri and the Goecha La. Spend two nights to see the village; much longer if you are trekking.

highlights.title: Norbugang coronation site
highlights.text: A stone throne, a chorten and an old cypress tree mark the place where the first Chogyal was consecrated in 1642. It is a short, gentle walk from the bazaar and a peaceful place at dawn.

highlights.title: Kathok lake
highlights.text: A small lake beside Norbugang, said to have been used for water in the coronation ceremony. Prayer flags ring the shore, and it reflects the forest on still mornings.

highlights.title: Dubdi monastery
highlights.text: About an hour's walk uphill through forest, Dubdi was founded in 1701 and is counted as Sikkim's oldest monastery. A small stone building with a quiet courtyard and wide views over the valley.

highlights.title: Trailhead for Goecha La
highlights.text: Yuksom is the start of the trek to Dzongri and Goecha La in Khangchendzonga National Park, one of the most popular high-altitude treks in the Himalaya, usually taking 8–11 days.

highlights.title: Village homestays
highlights.text: Small lodges and family homestays in Yuksom give simple, warm stays with home-cooked meals and time to watch the village go about its day.

field_notes.fact: In 1642 three lamas consecrated Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal of Sikkim at Yuksom, and the stone seat at Norbugang is remembered as the site of the coronation.
Dubdi monastery, on the ridge above Yuksom, was established in 1701 and is regarded as the first monastery built in Sikkim.
Khangchendzonga National Park was inscribed in 2016 as India's first mixed World Heritage Site, recognised for both its natural landscape and its sacred meaning to the people of Sikkim.

local_word.meaning: meeting place of the three lamas, the usual explanation of the village name

costs: Goecha La trek with agency, 8–11 days

how_to_reach.text: Yuksom is about 35 km from Pelling, 1.5–2 hours via the Rimbi and Kanchenjunga falls road. From Gangtok, it is about 140 km, 6–7 hours. Landslides are common in the monsoon; check current status before you travel.
Shared jeeps run from Gyalshing to Yuksom through the day and from Gangtok and Jorethang in the morning. Seats are cheap but departures can be slow to fill.
Bagdogra Airport is about 150 km away, 6–7 hours by road. Most travellers break the journey in Pelling.

where_to_stay: Saver: family homestays and simple lodges around the bazaar charge about ₹1,500–2,800 per person with meals, and trekkers' lodges are cheaper still. Comfort: a few small resorts and lodges with gardens and Kangchenjunga views sit on the edges of the village; ask your agency for current picks. There is no luxury hotel in Yuksom; signature trips usually stay in Pelling and visit for the day.
tips: Walk to Norbugang and Kathok lake at dawn, before the day trippers arrive from Pelling.
Wear good shoes for the walk to Dubdi; the trail is steep and slippery after rain.
Book Goecha La treks only with registered agencies; a licensed guide and park permit are needed.
Carry cash; Yuksom has limited or no reliable ATMs.
Leeches are common on forest paths from June to September; carry salt or repellent.

experiences.title: Norbugang and Kathok lake at dawn
experiences.summary: Walk from the bazaar to Norbugang, where the first Chogyal was consecrated in 1642, and the small Kathok lake beside it. At dawn, the stone throne, chorten and old cypress stand in quiet light, with prayer flags moving in the breeze.
body: Norbugang lies a short walk above the Yuksom bazaar, signposted from the main road. A stone throne stands under a large cypress tree, with a chorten and a small temple nearby. Tradition holds that the throne was the seat used during the consecration of Phuntsog Namgyal in 1642, and that the stone footprint beside it belongs to one of the lamas.

A few minutes' walk away, Kathok lake is a small pond ringed with prayer flags. It is said that water from the lake was used in the consecration ceremony. Today it is a quiet place where local families stop to pray and walk.

The best time to visit is early morning, before day visitors from Pelling arrive. Walk slowly, keep the chortens on your right and avoid sitting on the throne or shrines. In the evening, the light is soft and the village quiet, and the site is equally pleasant.

faqs.q: What is the Norbugang coronation throne?
faqs.a: A stone seat at Yuksom where tradition says the first Chogyal of Sikkim was consecrated in 1642. It stands under an old cypress tree, with a chorten and a small temple nearby.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Norbugang?
faqs.a: Usually no. It is a public site within the village, open in daylight hours. Respect the shrines and do not sit on the throne.

faqs.q: How far is Kathok lake from Norbugang?
faqs.a: A few minutes' walk. Most visitors see both on the same short walk from the Yuksom bazaar.

experiences.title: Hike to Dubdi, Sikkim's oldest monastery
experiences.summary: Climb through forest for about an hour to Dubdi, founded in 1701 and counted as Sikkim's oldest monastery. A small stone gompa on a ridge, with prayer flags, an old courtyard and views down over Yuksom and the valley.
body: The trail starts near the edge of Yuksom and climbs steeply through forest of oak, rhododendron and fern, with stone steps in places. Most walkers take 45 minutes to an hour to reach the monastery. In the monsoon, the path is slippery and leeches are common, so the dry months are best.

Dubdi was established in 1701, not long after the founding of the kingdom, and its name is often translated as the retreat. The monastery is a small two-storey stone building with a sloping roof, surrounded by prayer flags. Inside are statues and paintings associated with the Nyingma tradition.

The monastery may be locked if the caretaker is away, so ask in the village before you set out, or go with a local guide. Even if you cannot enter, the walk and the views make the climb worthwhile. Carry water and wear proper shoes.

faqs.q: How long is the hike to Dubdi monastery?
faqs.a: About 45 minutes to an hour uphill from Yuksom, and a little less coming down. Allow 2–3 hours in total with time at the monastery.
Not always. The caretaker may be away, so ask in Yuksom before you set out or go with a local guide who can check.
It is short but steep, with steps and roots on the path. Most reasonably fit walkers manage it. Avoid it after heavy rain, when the path is slippery.

experiences.title: The Goecha La trek from Yuksom
experiences.summary: Trek from Yuksom through Khangchendzonga National Park, via Sachen, Tshoka and Dzongri, to the viewpoints below the Goecha La, facing the east face of Kangchenjunga. It is a high, demanding trek that needs a registered agency, a licensed guide and good acclimatisation.
body: The trail leaves Yuksom and climbs through forest along the Prek Chu to Sachen and Tshoka, then up through rhododendron to Dzongri, at around 4,000 m, known for its sunrise view of Kangchenjunga and its neighbours. The route continues past Kokchurang and Thansing to Lamuney and the Samiti lake, then climbs before dawn to the viewpoints below the Goecha La.

Most itineraries take 8–11 days, and many groups turn around at View Point 1, at about 4,600 m, which is the usual high point for trekkers. The landscape changes from subtropical forest to alpine meadows, moraine and glacial lakes, all within a protected World Heritage Site. Teahouses are few; you camp or use simple trekkers' huts.

Treks must be booked with a registered agency, which arranges the park permits, a licensed guide, porters or yaks, and food. Foreigners need additional permits and must travel in groups. Altitude is a serious risk: build in rest days, ascend slowly and descend if symptoms worsen. Talk to your doctor before booking. Rules and fees change; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for Goecha La?
faqs.a: Yes. Treks into Khangchendzonga National Park must be organised through a registered agency with a licensed guide. The agency arranges the permits. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time for the Goecha La trek?
faqs.a: April to May for rhododendrons and October to November for the clearest views. Winter brings heavy snow, and the monsoon makes trails slippery and views rare.

faqs.q: How difficult is the Goecha La trek?
faqs.a: It is a demanding high-altitude trek, reaching about 4,600 m at View Point 1, with long days and steep climbs. Good fitness, proper gear and acclimatisation days are essential.
Yuksom is about 35 km from Pelling, 1.5–2 hours by road, and about 140 km from Gangtok. Shared jeeps run from Gyalshing and Jorethang; a private taxi from Pelling costs about ₹2,000–3,000.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Yuksom?
faqs.a: Indian nationals need no permit for Yuksom village. Foreigners need the Sikkim Restricted Area Permit. Treks into Khangchendzonga National Park, including Dzongri and Goecha La, need park and trekking permits arranged by a registered agency. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Yuksom?
faqs.a: March to May and October to December. The dry months are best for the walk to Dubdi and for treks. June to September brings heavy rain and leeches.

faqs.q: How many days should I spend in Yuksom?
faqs.a: Two nights cover Norbugang, Kathok lake and Dubdi at a relaxed pace. Trekkers need 8–11 days for Goecha La, plus a night before and after in Yuksom.
Yes, for a quiet stay. The village is small and walkable, and Norbugang and Kathok lake are easy outings. The Dubdi climb suits older children who walk well.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network in Yuksom?
faqs.a: There is some mobile coverage in the village, but it is patchy. Expect no signal on treks beyond Sachen.
ATMs in Yuksom are limited or unreliable. Withdraw cash in Gyalshing, Pelling or Gangtok before you arrive.
It was Sikkim's first capital, where the first Chogyal was consecrated in 1642. It is also known for Dubdi monastery and as the trailhead for the Goecha La and Dzongri treks.

faqs.q: How much does the Goecha La trek cost?
faqs.a: With a registered agency, expect about ₹15,000–30,000 per person for 8–11 days, including guide, food, tents and porters or yaks. Park fees, equipment rental and travel to Yuksom are usually extra.
